title: A Learned Policy Behind a Guard: Inputs Nobody Trained On, Outputs Past the Limit, and a Controller to Hand Over To

questions.question: A sensor sends a NaN for the heading. What should a guarded policy do?
options: Pass it to the network, which will ignore it
Hand over to the fall-back with that input taken as zero, and record why
Stop the program
Use the last heading for ever
questions.explanation: A NaN through a network comes out as anything. The guard keeps it out and says it did.

questions.question: From the wide starts, how did the clone do without and with the guard?
options: 98 percent without and 87 with
98 percent both times
87 percent without and 98 percent with, the guard handing over on 12 percent of the steps
The same, since the network is unchanged
questions.explanation: The guard hands over near the edges, where the clone was never taught.

questions.question: From the narrow starts, on what share of the steps did the guard hand over?
options: 2.4 percent
12 percent
All of them
20 percent
questions.explanation: Where the network was taught, the guard lets it drive.

questions.question: With a threshold of 1 spread, what happened?
options: The guard handed over on 0 percent and the clone failed as before
Nothing changed
The success fell to zero
The guard handed over on 20 percent of the steps, taking that much of the driving from the network, and succeeded on 98 percent
questions.explanation: The fall-back here is as good as the expert, so success held; the cost was driving the network was trained to do.

questions.question: Why is the fall-back a plain controller written by hand?
options: Because it can be checked by reading it, which is why it is trusted where the network is not
Because it is always better than the network
Because networks cannot be used twice
Because it was trained on more data
questions.explanation: Its job is to be predictable where the network may not be, not to be the best everywhere.

questions.question: What is the weakness of a box of spreads round the training data as a test of unseen states?
options: It costs too much to compute
A state inside the box can still be far from any sample, in a corner the data never reached
It rejects every state
It only works with two inputs
questions.explanation: A box is the simplest test. Distance to the nearest samples is a better one, and none is perfect.
